world_behind.title: Some of them believed
world_behind.text: Verse 1 is easy to read past. Many believed, repented, and began to search the scriptures. The chapter that follows is about the rest, and the record makes sure the reader knows the preaching worked before it reports what it cost.

world_behind.title: The charge is reviling the law
world_behind.text: Verse 5 has the people witnessing that Alma and Amulek reviled the law and the lawyers and judges. Amulek had said in so many words that he spoke in favor of their law (Alma 10:26). The trial proceeds on the accusation the accused already answered.

world_behind.title: Zeezrom breaks first, and publicly
world_behind.text: He does not slip away. He takes the guilt on himself and clears the prisoners aloud, pleads for them, and is spat on and cast out for it. His conversion costs him the city inside a single verse.

world_behind.title: The records burn with the people
world_behind.text: Verse 8 puts the holy scriptures into the same fire as the wives and children. A city destroying its own text alongside those who believe it is a detail the record chose to keep, and it makes the burning an act against memory as much as against persons.

world_behind.title: The judge belongs to Nehor
world_behind.text: Verse 16 identifies him with the order and faith of Nehor, who killed Gideon in Alma 1. The record ties this scene back to the first chapter of the book, so the reader knows the priestcraft introduced there is now sitting on a bench.

world_behind.title: Prison here is deprivation
world_behind.text: They are struck, questioned, mocked for days, denied food and water, and stripped. The record lists the treatment plainly and without adjectives, and the list runs several days long.

world_behind.title: The date is given to the day
world_behind.text: Verse 23 supplies the twelfth day of the tenth month of the tenth year. The record dates the deliverance the way it dated Amulek's conversion four chapters ago, fixing the moment to the day.

words.text: Secretly, out of sight. In the King James Bible it is the word for laying an ambush: lurking, waiting for blood, bringing in false teachers unnoticed. It has one famous gentle use, when Joseph is minded to put Mary away privily to spare her. Ammonihah "sought to put them away privily" (v. 3) in the same construction and the opposite spirit.

cites.quote: sought to put them away privily

spans.text: sought to put them away privily

words.text: Awareness of one's own state. The word appears five times in this record and never in the King James Bible. Zeezrom's soul is harrowed up "under a consciousness of his own guilt" (v. 6), and what he is conscious of is named precisely. The record saves the word for people who have just understood what they did.

cites.quote: under a consciousness of his own guilt

spans.text: under a consciousness of his own guilt

words.text: Without blemish, the old requirement for anything offered. Treated at 2 Nephi 33:7. Zeezrom says "I am guilty, and these men are spotless before God" (v. 7), which is a sacrificial word applied to two men about to be bound. The sentence divides the room into one man who knows what he is and two who are about to be treated as offerings.

cites.quote: I am guilty, and these men are spotless before God

spans.text: I am guilty, and these men are spotless before God

words.text: Death for a testimony, and here the name of a place: they were carried "to the place of martyrdom" (v. 9). The word is absent from the King James Bible and appears twice in this record. Its use as an address implies a city with a customary spot for this.

Grinding the teeth, the gesture of rage in the older books and of torment in the gospels. Here the tormentors do it while asking "How shall we look when we are damned?" (v. 21), which puts the gesture of the damned on the faces of the people mocking. The record does not comment on the irony.

cites.quote: How shall we look when we are damned?

spans.text: How shall we look when we are damned?

words.text: Two. Treated at 2 Nephi 16:2. The walls of the prison "were rent in twain" (v. 27), and rent in twain is the exact phrase Matthew uses of the temple veil at the crucifixion. Both are barriers torn from top to bottom at a moment of death, and in both the tearing is what people see first.

phrases.term: Began to repent, and to search the scriptures
phrases.text: The first thing the chapter reports is success. Belief, repentance, and then reading, in that order. The verse also explains where the church at Sidom later in this book comes from.

phrases.term: I am guilty, and these men are spotless before God
phrases.text: Zeezrom's whole conversion in one sentence, and it takes the form of public testimony. He confesses in public, on the record, to the people he misled. What it earns him is spitting and expulsion.

phrases.term: The Spirit constraineth me that I must not stretch forth mine hand
phrases.text: The hardest sentence in the chapter, and it is a restraint, not an inability. Alma has the power and is being held back from using it. The verse gives the reason without softening it: the Lord receives them in glory, and the deed is being allowed so that the judgments may be just.

phrases.term: Our work is not finished; therefore they burn us not
phrases.text: Alma's answer to whether they will die too, and it puts survival on usefulness. The same logic would have burned them the moment the work ended. Amulek gets no promise of safety, only of timing.

phrases.term: This judge was after the order and faith of Nehor
phrases.text: A single verse of identification that reaches back thirteen chapters. Nehor was executed in Alma 1 and his teaching outlived him well enough to seat a judge. The record is tracking an idea.

phrases.term: How shall we look when we are damned?
phrases.text: Said in mockery, and it is the chapter's grimmest line. They are quoting the doctrine back as a taunt while doing the thing it warns about. Nobody in the scene hears it as a question.

phrases.term: How long shall we suffer these great afflictions, O Lord?
phrases.text: The prayer that ends the imprisonment, and it opens with a complaint. Alma asks how long before he asks for strength, and the record keeps the complaint in. The petition that follows is for strength unto deliverance.

phrases.term: According to their faith which was in Christ
phrases.text: The explanation given twice in three verses. The power that broke the cords is credited to faith, and the object of the faith is named both times. The record is careful not to let the miracle stand on its own.

verses.label: v. 10–11
verses.title: A request refused, with the reason given at once
verses.text: The record preserves Amulek's proposal in his own words: "How can we witness this awful scene? Therefore let us stretch forth our hands, and exercise the power of God which is in us, and save them from the flames." The refusal names its constraint and then its purpose: "The Spirit constraineth me that I must not stretch forth mine hand; for behold the Lord receiveth them up unto himself, in glory... that the judgments which he shall exercise upon them in his wrath may be just." The reason offered is about the persecutors' sentencing, not about the victims.

verses.label: v. 12–13
verses.title: A fear stated and a prediction with a stated basis
verses.text: Amulek says the obvious thing: "Behold, perhaps they will burn us also." The answer accepts the possibility and then denies it on grounds that can be checked against the rest of the book: "Be it according to the will of the Lord. But, behold, our work is not finished; therefore they burn us not." A character makes a falsifiable claim about his own survival inside the scene, and the reason he gives is a piece of work still outstanding.

verses.label: v. 17–22
verses.title: What was said, and what was not
verses.text: The record keeps both sides of the silence. "Alma and Amulek answered him nothing" (v. 17), and again in verse 18 they "answered him nothing." Against that it preserves the taunts as speech: "Know ye not that I have power to deliver you up unto the flames?" and "How shall we look when we are damned?" Verse 22 sums the treatment in physical terms, gnashing, spitting, mocking "for many days," and food and water withheld. The two prisoners contribute no dialogue at all for six verses.

cites.quote: Alma and Amulek answered him nothing

spans.text: Alma and Amulek answered him nothing

verses.label: v. 23
verses.title: The most precise date in the book, in brackets
verses.text: One parenthesis fixes the moment to the day: "(and it was on the twelfth day, in the tenth month, in the tenth year of the reign of the judges over the people of Nephi)." Only ten verses in the whole volume name a numbered day of a month, and this is the only one in the Ammonihah episode. The precision arrives at the point where the imprisonment ends, and the sentence around it is otherwise a plain report of the chief judge coming in to smite them again.

chapter.title: The miracle is withheld first and given later
chapter.text: Verse 10 has the request made explicitly, "let us stretch forth our hands, and exercise the power of God which is in us," and verse 11 has it refused with a reason, "The Spirit constraineth me that I must not stretch forth mine hand." Sixteen verses later the same power arrives, and verse 28 states the ground in the same terms as the refusal, "the Lord had granted unto them power, according to their faith which was in Christ." The withholding and the granting are attributed to one source in one chapter, and the withholding comes first.

chapter.title: The reason given is judgment
chapter.text: Alma says the deed is suffered so that the judgments upon the city may be just. It is a hard answer and the record supplies no softer one, then spends the next chapter and a half carrying it out.

chapter.title: Silence is the response to interrogation
chapter.text: Alma and Amulek answer nothing, repeatedly, over days. Amulek argued in chapter 10 and Alma preached in 12 and 13. Here the record shows two men who have said everything they were sent to say.

chapter.title: Zeezrom's conversion is complete before the chapter is half over
chapter.text: He accuses himself, defends the innocent, and is expelled. The book's most thorough turn belongs to the man who tried hardest to buy a denial.

chapter.title: The record keeps the complaint
chapter.text: Alma's prayer begins by asking how long. The book could have kept only the request for strength. It preserves the exhaustion in front of it.

chapter.title: Nehor is the through-line
chapter.text: Alma 1 introduced the teaching, Alma 14 finds it on the judgment seat and in the prison. The record is showing what an idea does over thirteen chapters.

chapter.title: Everything burned is replaceable except the people
chapter.text: Verse 8 lists what was burned without a break, "wives and children" and "their records which contained the holy scriptures." The record puts the books in the same clause as the people and does not comment. Alma 16:9–11 reports the city destroyed "in one day" and renamed Desolation of Nehors, and Alma 16:2 dates it to the eleventh year, two chapters and roughly three years later. The burning of a text and the erasure of the city that burned it are recorded without a word connecting them.

applications.title: Confess to the people you misled
applications.text: Zeezrom did it out loud, to the crowd he had deceived, "Behold, I am guilty, and these men are spotless before God," and it cost him: they reviled him and cast him out. A private acknowledgment would have been easier and would not have been the same act.

applications.title: Accept that you may be held back
applications.text: Amulek asked to use the power and Alma refused with a reason, "The Spirit constraineth me that I must not stretch forth mine hand." When you are able to fix something and something in you says not to, that is a recognized position in this book and not a failure of faith.

applications.title: Say what you can see rather than what you can explain
applications.text: Alma does not account for why the fire is permitted. He states what he knows, that the Lord "receiveth them up unto himself, in glory," and that the blood will stand as a witness. When you cannot answer the question, say the part you can and stop there.

applications.title: Say nothing when you have said everything
applications.text: Silence under questioning is a real answer here, chosen by men who had already spoken, and the record repeats it twice, "Alma and Amulek answered him nothing." Notice the difference between not having a reply and having finished giving one.

applications.title: Notice how long the ordinary part lasts
applications.text: Between the burning and the deliverance the record puts many days of mockery, spitting, hunger and thirst, and then a precise date, "the twelfth day, in the tenth month, in the tenth year." Most of what is endured in this chapter is not dramatic, and the record counts it anyway.

applications.title: Let the complaint into the prayer
applications.text: The record keeps "How long shall we suffer these great afflictions, O Lord?" in front of the petition. Try praying the honest first sentence before the acceptable second one, and see whether the second changes.

applications.title: Ask according to a specified object
applications.text: The request is "give us strength according to our faith which is in Christ," and verse 28 reports the outcome in the same words. The faith in this chapter is never left as a general disposition; it always has something named after it.

applications.title: Walk out and keep walking
applications.text: They came forth unhurt and the record says they "straightway came forth out of the prison," and Alma 15:1 has them leaving the city entirely. A deliverance is not the same as a vindication, and this one does not stop to collect an apology.

questions.text: When did a hard word actually work on me, and did I ever tell the person who said it?
What would I have to say in public, to people who heard me say the opposite, for a change in me to be real?
When have I been restrained from fixing something, and did I treat that as guidance or as failure?
If my safety lasts as long as my work does, what work am I actually doing?
What true thing have I repeated as a joke because taking it seriously would cost me something?
What is my honest first sentence to God right now, before the respectable one?
What have I credited to luck or timing that I would describe differently if I were being exact?
